1335.bp: When you shop online, you see recommendations based on what you've already clicked or bought. But the best opportunities are often the things you want but haven't consciously looked for yet—like discovering you need a new jacket in summer before you actively search for it. The real goal is to wake up those hidden desires early, before a customer even realizes they have them, so they find things they actually want to buy.
1335.wh: Generative systems that make recommendations work by predicting from a vocabulary of product IDs based purely on behavioral patterns—clicks and purchases. This means they're reactive: they can only activate what they've seen you do before. If a customer has a latent need that hasn't shown up in their action history yet, the system has no signal to work with, so it stays silent. This creates a cold-start problem: you can't recommend what you haven't explicitly seen someone demand.
1335.ap: The team built a two-stage system. Offline, they use a large language model (a neural network trained on text to reason about language and concepts) to think about what hidden needs a customer might have based on their profile, then teach a smaller, faster model to mimic that reasoning. Online, when a customer searches or browses, the system takes those predicted hidden needs, converts them into the same product-ID vocabulary the recommender understands, and feeds them into the recommendation decoder alongside the behavioral signals. Then they fine-tune the recommender using a technique called GRPO that balances exploring new intent-aligned options while not forgetting what actually drives purchases.
1335.ww: A large language model can reason about human needs from textual context—it understands concepts, context, and latent desires in ways that pure behavioral data can't. By distilling that reasoning into a lightweight model and injecting it as a bridge between free-form thinking and the system's native product-ID language, you expand the search space without breaking the tight latency budget of real-time serving. The KL regularization prevents the model from chasing hypothetical intents so hard it forgets to actually recommend things people will buy.
1335.po: The system increases the density and diversity of recommendations that align with hidden user intents without significantly reducing recall of real past behavior. This means customers see more things they actually want, discovered before they actively searched for them, while the platform still hits things they were definitely interested in.

1336.bp: In e-commerce search, what matters most is that the products shown match both what the customer searched for *and* their taste. A person searching for 'shoes' needs not just grammatically correct matches but shoes they'll actually buy—ones that fit their budget, style, and history. The challenge is that product images, descriptions, and text all carry meaning that numbers alone can't capture, so you need to weave multiple types of information together.
1336.wh: Existing systems fine-tune one general multimodal AI (a model that reads images, text, audio together) on a single behavioral signal—usually clicks. But in real e-commerce, what makes a shoe good varies: sometimes customers click to compare, sometimes to add to cart, sometimes just to read reviews. Using one signal leaves money on the table. And when you take the output representations (learned patterns) and feed them to a ranking model, the ranking system treats them like any other feature—it doesn't exploit the rich structure inside those multimodal learnings.
1336.ap: They built a single architecture that fine-tunes a multimodal model using many signals at once—clicks, add-to-cart, purchases—each with its own specialized tokens and output layers within a shared backbone. In a single pass, this generates rich product representations that encode all those signals. Then in the ranking model, instead of just using these as static features, they build task-specific user representations by watching how a user's *search behavior* sequences through products, using the multimodal signals to understand the user more deeply.
1336.ww: A single shared backbone learning from multiple signals simultaneously captures how those signals relate to each other—a click doesn't mean the same thing as a purchase, and the model learns those distinctions. When you then use those learned patterns to build user representations from behavior sequences, you're leveraging that multi-signal understanding to build a richer picture of who the user is. This beats training one model per signal or treating representations as passive features.
1336.po: The system achieves both better ranking quality and faster inference compared to methods that use single signals or treat multimodal data naively. Real deployment shows the approach works at scale.

1337.bp: Search ranking has a fundamental tension in e-commerce: optimize for what people click on right now, and you end up promoting popular items that might not actually match what they searched for. Optimize for semantic quality—does the product match the search intent—and you might hurt engagement. The real goal is managing that tradeoff explicitly so that a ranking model can balance discovering genuinely relevant things while still driving business metrics.
1337.wh: Industrial search models typically optimize for immediate engagement signals alone—clicks, purchases, dwell time. This creates a bias toward popular, price-anchored, or flashy items. But semantic relevance—whether the product actually answers the customer's question—is invisible to the model. You can't balance something you're not measuring. And getting reliable relevance labels at scale is hard; human raters can't judge 100 million search-product pairs.
1337.ap: They built a multi-task ranking model with two heads: one predicts ordinal relevance (irrelevant, moderately relevant, highly relevant) and preserves the natural ordering of those categories, and another head predicts engagement signals. A unified scoring function combines both, letting operators dial in the tradeoff. To label 100 million pairs, they use a lightweight fine-tuned large language model to generate three-level relevance judgments automatically, validated against human annotations to ensure reliability.
1337.ww: By explicitly modeling relevance as an ordinal ranking (preserving the order of the categories) rather than a binary or flat problem, you capture the structure of what relevance means. Combining it with engagement through a unified score lets you pull both levers—when you optimize with both signals, you naturally get items that are both more relevant to the query and still drive engagement, because the model learns when they align and when they conflict. Pre-labeling at scale with a validated lightweight LLM avoids the need for millions of human judgments.
1337.po: Offline metrics like NDCG improve (a measure of ranking quality), and online A/B tests show the system improves semantic alignment while preserving or improving engagement objectives. Customers see more relevant results without sacrificing business impact.

1338.bp: Modern e-commerce isn't just keyword matching anymore; customers arrive with complex needs like 'show me dresses suitable for office but also casual Fridays.' Large language models are good at breaking down these complex intents and building multi-step plans. But if a model plans without knowing what products are actually in the inventory right now, or what the search engine can actually retrieve, its plan might be impossible to execute. The real challenge is planning smartly in real time without the seconds of latency that iterative planning entails.
1338.wh: Query-rewriting systems that rephrase searches are agnostic to what's actually in stock or searchable—they might rewrite 'office-casual dress' into something the search engine can't find. Deep reasoning agents that iteratively probe the environment and revise their plans work better but are too slow: each plan-check-revise loop adds latency, and industrial search has to work in under a second. You're stuck between plans that are theoretically good but practically impossible, and plans that are safe but slow.
1338.ap: They restructured planning into three stages. First, offline, a teacher agent uses the retrieval system's own API to probe what's actually available, then synthesizes valid execution plans—plans that it's verified can actually work. The agent learns from its failures to understand what makes a plan executable. Second, they train a lightweight planner (a neural model) on those offline-validated plans using supervised learning. Third, during deployment, the planner runs once with no iteration—it gets a fast snapshot of what's in inventory, reasons about what's achievable, and outputs a single plan in milliseconds.
1338.ww: By doing the environment-awareness offline—discovering what works and what doesn't before deploying—you collapse a feedback loop. The deployed planner doesn't need to iterate; it's learned the structure of feasible plans. Probing the inventory once in real time gives the planner concrete ground truth without the latency cost of iterative reasoning. This inverts the traditional agent architecture: instead of plan-then-probe-then-revise, it's probe-once-then-plan-once.
1338.po: The system can resolve complex multi-faceted user intents (like the office-casual dress example) with a single fast planning step, staying within the sub-second latency budget of industrial e-commerce while ensuring the recommended search plan is actually executable with the current inventory.

1339.bp: Video search is fundamentally different from text or product search: a user watches a video for seconds or minutes before deciding it's what they want, but search rankings must be decided in milliseconds. And personalization is key—the same query means different things to different people based on their viewing history. The goal is to rewrite vague or broad queries into something more specific to that particular user's interests, but without delay.
1339.wh: Generic large language models can rewrite queries, but they ignore what individual users care about—they produce the same rewrite for everyone. Naive personalization methods that add user history features can dilute the signal with noise or become too slow to serve. And deciding when to personalize is hard: for some queries, being vague is fine; for others, it's essential. You need to know which case you're in to make the effort worthwhile.
1339.ap: WeWrite has three components. First, a data-mining stage that looks backward through a user's history and automatically flags scenarios where personalization would help most (high-quality, high-impact rewrites). Second, training the rewriter using supervised fine-tuning on those flagged cases, then reinforcement learning to ensure the rewrites align with how the video search system ranks results. Third, a parallel system architecture during deployment that serves both a personalized rewrite and a fallback lightweight rewrite in parallel, so latency stays low.
1339.wh: By identifying when personalization matters—rather than personalizing everything—you avoid wasting compute and quality on cases where a generic rewrite is fine. Combining supervised learning with reinforcement learning ensures the rewrites don't just sound good; they actually improve what the video search system retrieves. Parallel serving means you're never choosing between personalization and speed.
1339.po: The system improved rewriting accuracy by over 27% compared to general large language models. Deployed in WeChat (a platform with 1+ billion users), it increased video views by 1.07% and reduced query re-formulation (frustrated users searching again) by 2.97%.

1340.bp: Recommendation systems learn from sequences of what users do—the order they browse, what they click. This works well because real user journeys evolve and deepen: you watch a funny video, then related recommendations lead you to more humor, then maybe to a specific comedian. But user history is messy and fragmented: the same person might click on cooking content one day and gaming content the next, and those are totally unrelated. A model that tries to understand both at once gets confused, like trying to follow a conversation when two people keep interrupting each other.
1340.wh: Current models treat the entire user history as a single chronological sequence—like a sentence in a text-language model. But user history isn't a sentence; it's more like a filing cabinet with multiple folders. When you force everything into one sequence, unrelated behaviors compete for the model's attention budget. This 'context pollution' means the model can't clearly see the coherent patterns within each interest, so it misses opportunities to recommend things the user actually wants.
1340.ap: CMSL introduces a learning module that actively reconstructs user history into multiple separate, coherent sequences—each representing a pure thematic strand of interest. Instead of one long messy sequence, you might end up with one sequence for cooking videos, another for gaming, another for fitness. A linear attention mechanism then efficiently models each strand. The system learns which behaviors belong to which strand automatically, without manual labeling.
1340.wh: By disentangling user history into thematic strands, you remove the noise that masks clear patterns. Each sequence becomes more like a real sentence—coherent and logical. Linear attention (a simpler, faster form of learning patterns) works well on clean thematic sequences because the patterns are stronger. The result is that the model can see high-intent patterns much more clearly.
1340.po: The system captures temporal user-behavior nuances better than treating history as a monolithic sequence, improving recommendation quality by reducing the dilution effect of unrelated behaviors.

1341.bp: When you buy something online, that purchase often marks the end of wanting that thing—you now own a jacket, so you don't need to shop for jackets again. But your need will eventually return—next year you'll want a new jacket. The tension is that normal recommendation models treat purchases the same as clicks (interest signals), not realizing that a purchase should temporarily suppress recommendations for that item category while tracking when you'll want to buy again.
1341.wh: Sequential recommendation models are built to accumulate signals: more clicks and purchases mean stronger preference. But this breaks down after purchase. A purchase isn't like a click; it's an 'interest exit'—the fulfillment of a temporary need. If you keep recommending jackets right after a customer just bought one, you waste impressions and annoy users. And because purchases look like engagement to the model, they strengthen the pattern, making the problem worse. Current models have no way to understand that the lifecycle of an interest—from dormant to active to satisfied to dormant again—differs fundamentally from a continuous preference.
1341.ap: SAM models interest lifecycle explicitly through several mechanisms. First, when a purchase occurs, a cross-attention mechanism looks back through the history and suppresses the earlier clicks related to that purchase (recognizing the purchase fulfilled that intent). It also retrieves replenishment rhythms—how often similar customers rebuy similar items. Second, an adaptive gating unit creates a soft mask that immediately silences recommendations for satisfied categories, but gradually relaxes this mask as the predicted rebuy time approaches. Third, a self-supervised training task learns the natural product lifecycle (time-to-next-purchase) from raw purchase data, without needing humans to label it.
1341.ww: Explicitly modeling when an interest is satisfied and when it will re-activate captures the true dynamics of e-commerce. Rather than fighting the model's default behavior (accumulation), you build lifecycle awareness into its architecture. The self-supervised auxiliary task lets the model learn product replenishment patterns from the data itself, scaling to any product category automatically. The gradual reactivation (rather than sudden switching) matches human behavior: as a lifecycle approaches, you naturally become more receptive to that product category again.
1341.po: The system reduces the post-purchase repeat-rate (showing the same product after a purchase) by over 60%, dramatically improving user experience by showing relevant things at the right time in their lifecycle.

1342.bp: Generative recommendation systems produce recommendations as sequences of product IDs, like a language model writes sentences. These systems learn patterns from historical data, but the world changes—new products arrive, user interests shift, and behavioral patterns evolve. Keeping a model current is a constant tension: retrain from scratch and you lose what you learned, losing stability; fine-tune on new data and you risk forgetting the old patterns and overfitting to recent trends that might not be stable.
1342.wh: Full retraining on a sliding window of data is expensive and slow; by the time you finish retraining, the world has moved on again. Incremental fine-tuning on recent data is fast but risky: your model might adapt too heavily to what happened last week (which could be a blip) or forget general preferences that still matter. And the distribution of users changes over time: power users who interact constantly need different serving strategies than casual users. A one-size-fits-all serving approach either under-adapts for active users or over-adapts for casual ones.
1342.ap: They propose a hybrid approach: maintain a stable base model trained on a long history of data, apply lightweight fine-tuning (tuning a small number of parameters) on recent interactions to create an updated model, and at serving time, route users with fresh signals to the updated model while serving others with the stable base model. This splits the user base and the model portfolio: active users get rapid adaptation, while the bulk of users stay on the stable model.
1342.wh: By maintaining two models with different objectives, you avoid forcing a single model to be both stable and adaptive. The base model anchors to long-term patterns, so you don't forget what's been consistently true. The updated model is allowed to shift based on recent weeks without affecting the base. Routing decisions at serving time mean active users—who have the most recent and reliable signals—get the most recent adaptation, while users with sparse history stay on the proven base model. This is more robust than trying to balance stability and adaptation in a single model.
1342.po: The system handles model updating in dynamic e-commerce environments without the expense of full retraining or the instability of naive fine-tuning, supporting both rapid adaptation for active users and stability for the broader population.

1343.bp: Video and content platforms face a multi-task ranking problem: should they recommend something because users will click it (quick win), or because they'll watch it for a long time (engagement), or because it fits their interests (retention)? These goals can conflict—a clickbait title gets clicks but short watch time. The system needs to model all three simultaneously rather than juggling them separately, wasting compute and creating conflicting signals.
1343.wh: Independent models for each task mean redundant computation and missed opportunities to learn how tasks relate. For instance, a video that gets long watch time and low click might tell you something about the thumbnails that a single-task model can't discover. Multi-task learning can help, but applying it to generative retrieval—where you're sequentially generating product IDs—is tricky because you need to use language model structure to handle multiple prediction heads efficiently without slowing down inference.
1343.ap: RedGR builds a generative retrieval model with unified multi-task capabilities. It generates sequences of product IDs while simultaneously predicting clicks, dwell-time, and engagement behaviors. They refine the mechanism that maps semantic product identifiers to concrete items, ensuring that the retrieval actually returns what the predictions intended. Multi-task learning happens within the decoder-only architecture, so you get efficiency: one forward pass, multiple predictions.
1343.wh: By unifying task modeling within a generative framework, you reduce redundant computation and let the model learn how tasks interact. A single sequence generation process is inherently efficient compared to running separate models. Refining the ID-to-item mapping ensures theoretical predictions translate to actual retrieved items, closing a gap in prior generative retrieval systems.
1343.po: The system handles multiple recommendation objectives (clicks, dwell time, engagement) efficiently in a unified generative retrieval model without the computational overhead of independent models, improving both efficiency and effectiveness in video/content recommendation.

1344.bp: New content on social platforms arrives constantly—a new creator, a new video, a new trend. Within hours, you need to decide if it's worth recommending. But without history, you have almost no signal: no user interaction data, no click-through patterns, nothing to learn from. You're flying blind, yet recommendations matter enormously for newly-minted creators and for helping users discover emerging trends. The goal is to make smart early bets on new content despite having almost no data.
1344.wh: Traditional recommenders learn from user interactions: clicks, watches, likes. But new content has zero interactions. You could explore randomly—show it to some users and see what happens—but that's slow and wastes impressions. Or you could use content metadata (tags, descriptions), but that's often sparse or wrong for new posts. You need a way to judge quality before anyone has seen it, using just the content itself.
1344.ap: They use a large language model as a Bayesian prior builder. The LLM reads the content (images, captions, video frames) and assesses semantic quality and engagement potential purely from the content, producing a 'confidence' score before any user sees it. This score becomes the starting prior (initial belief) for an exploration-exploitation algorithm called Upper Confidence Bound (UCB). Early impressions are allocated based on this LLM-derived prior, and as real user interactions arrive, the algorithm gradually shifts away from the prior and toward observed data. They apply this at a reranking layer on top of a base ranker to avoid disrupting existing systems.
1344.wh: An LLM can reason about content quality from semantics alone—a video's topic, tone, and appeal—without needing interaction data. Framing this as a Bayesian prior means you start with informed uncertainty, not blind randomness. As interaction data arrives, the exploration gradually shifts toward exploitation, so good content still gets allocations even before massive interaction volume. Applying this as a reranking layer on top of a base ranker ensures integration without system overhaul.
1344.po: The system enables efficient exploration and discovery of cold-start content using LLM-derived semantic priors, improving user experience by surfacing emerging creators and trends while maintaining relevance through a base ranker.

1345.bp: Users often type vague queries because they can't predict what terminology the e-commerce system uses. They might search for 'nice watch' when the system indexes products as 'automatic stainless-steel chronograph'. This intent gap—the gap between what users search for and what they actually want—drives high abandonment. The goal is to bridge this gap by reasoning about who the user is and what they really want, then reformulating their query into something the search system will understand.
1345.wh: Personalization usually requires restructuring the entire ranking system architecture. Conversely, pure query rewriting ignores the user; it just rewrites the query text. What you need is a personalized rewrite—taking the user's history into account—but without costly architectural changes. And you need it fast, because users won't wait for complex reasoning during search.
1345.ap: They built an agentic system using ReAct (a reasoning framework that lets models think through steps and take actions). The agent analyzes a user's historical purchase and search data, reasons about what they might really be looking for, and reformulates the query into personalized terms. They pre-compute top likely reformulations offline to avoid latency, then at query time use fast similarity matching to find the best pre-computed version. The system sits on top of any existing search backend, so it integrates without rewiring anything.
1345.wh: By pre-computing and using matching rather than generative rewriting at query time, you get the reasoning power of agentic AI without latency. Sitting on top of existing systems means seamless integration—no downtime, no architectural changes. Historical purchase data grounds personalization in actual past behavior rather than guessing.
1345.po: The system significantly improves search ranking and customer engagement by bridging the intent gap, transforming vague queries into personalized, precise ones that the search system can match effectively.

1346.bp: Click-through prediction is the foundation of ad targeting and recommendation ranking: predict whether a user will click on an ad or product. But traditional models make local decisions—for each user-item pair, they predict click probability independently. This misses the bigger picture: users have evolving interests over time, and items fit into trajectories. A user interested in hiking boots one week then camping gear the next is following a coherent interest path. Models that miss this global pattern can't fully understand behavior.
1346.wh: Discriminative models (which optimize local decision boundaries for each prediction) work fast but can't see how all a user's interests connect. Generative models (which try to model the full distribution of interests over time) could capture global patterns, but existing approaches convert nuanced purchase signals into coarse categories, losing information in the process. You lose the topological richness of the interest trajectory—how smoothly interests evolve versus how suddenly they shift.
1346.ap: NIF models user intent as a continuous trajectory flowing across a high-dimensional manifold (a smooth geometric space). They enforce two kinematic constraints: Interest Diversity (different directions in the space mean different types of interests) and Evolution Velocity (smoothness, so interests don't jump randomly). Rather than discretizing signals into categories, they preserve the continuous structure. To handle the mismatch between generative pre-training and discriminative fine-tuning, they add a synchronization layer. A Temporal Sequential Pairwise mechanism instills temporal causality during fine-tuning.
1346.wh: Modeling interests as continuous flows on a geometric manifold preserves the topological fidelity of how interests actually evolve—smoothly for some users, with sharp transitions for others. The kinematic constraints capture the structure of interest dynamics naturally. By synchronizing between generative pre-training and discriminative fine-tuning explicitly, you avoid throwing away the global structure learned pre-training. Temporal causality ensures the model doesn't predict effects before causes.
1346.po: The system models user-intent evolution more faithfully than discriminative approaches, capturing both global transition patterns and local click probabilities, improving click-through prediction by understanding interests as evolving trajectories.

1347.bp: News platforms serve millions of articles a day, and each article has an image, headline, and text. Recommending articles using dense vector search (converting each article into a 1000-dimensional number) is accurate but expensive: storing and searching vectors takes memory and CPU. The real goal is to keep recommendation quality high while dramatically cutting the computational cost so you can serve recommendations faster and cheaper.
1347.wh: Dense float vectors capture semantic meaning well, but at scale they become a bottleneck. Searching a million articles with float vectors is slow. If you switch to binary codes (representing each article as a string of 1s and 0s), they're vastly faster and smaller, but they lose information. Finding a sweet spot where you keep most of the quality while gaining the speed benefits is the challenge.
1347.ap: They built a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 uses a learned binary projection—a neural transformation that converts float vectors into binary codes while preserving which articles are neighbors of which. It's trained with a contrastive objective (making similar items binary-close and dissimilar items binary-far). Stage 2 reranks the binary shortlist with float vectors to catch any quality loss. They evaluated on real-world tasks: top-20 recommendations (where you need to catch most of the good items) and top-5 precision (where you need near-perfect accuracy).
1347.wh: Training the binary projection with a contrastive objective means the binary codes preserve the geometric structure of the original vector space. By reranking the binary shortlist, you recover most quality while keeping stage 1 fast. Using real news articles (47,300 from NDTV) and real production scenarios grounds the approach in actual needs.
1347.po: The system achieves 95% recall of float-exact neighbors at moderate bit-widths (1024 bits) and 98% top-20 recall at the recommended operating point (3072 bits), delivering 4-6x speedup at million-scale without significantly sacrificing recommendation quality.

1348.bp: Technical documentation search (finding answers in software manuals) faces a vocabulary problem: users say 'Windows Server' while the docs call it 'ONTAP'. Users abbreviate, use legacy names, or misremember. Traditional search systems using controlled vocabularies can't bridge this gap. The goal is to translate everyday user language into the system's canonical terms so retrieval works reliably even when users don't speak the system's terminology.
1348.wh: Search indices use controlled vocabularies for consistency. But users don't know or follow controlled vocabularies; they use whatever terms make sense to them. If a user searches for 'WAFL' (an old NetApp acronym) and the docs only mention its modern name 'ONTAP', retrieval fails. Building a neural model to learn this mapping requires labeled training data at scale, which is expensive. The mismatch persists silently, users get poor answers, and they give up.
1348.ap: They use curated product-name artifacts—manually maintained lists of product names, abbreviations, and legacy terms mapped to canonical names. Two techniques leverage this curation. First, at query time, a normalizer rewrites the user query by mapping informal mentions to canonical names and adding latest version identifiers. Second, a product-scope filter dynamically builds structured retrieval constraints from a product catalog, restricting retrieval to documented products. Together, these lightweight techniques close the vocabulary gap without retraining any model.
1348.wh: By using curated knowledge rather than learned models, you avoid the data collection burden and gain maintainability: when a new product version launches, you update the curated list, not retrain a model. Normalizing at query time means every search benefits. Building structured filter expressions from the catalog ensures you're not searching against products that don't have documentation.
1348.po: On real production queries from docs.netapp.com, curated normalization improved Mean Reciprocal Rank (a measure of how high good results rank) by 42% with BM25 and 24-31% with dense retrievers, without retraining any model.

1349.bp: Searching for music is harder than it seems: users misspell song titles, transpose them, or phonetically scramble them. Amazon Music has 100+ million tracks, so the search system must handle real-world messiness at scale. The challenge is retrieval that's both semantically meaningful (understanding intent) and robust to surface-level noise (misspellings, variations).
1349.wh: Traditional n-gram matching (looking for character sequences) handles surface variations but is noisy and semantically weak. You'd retrieve things that match character sequences but are irrelevant. Dense semantic search (modern neural approaches) is semantically stronger but breaks on misspellings—the vectors don't account for surface form variations. Neural sparse retrieval (learning which sparse word-like units matter) could bridge this, but the standard approach memorizes lexical patterns rather than learning genuine robustness.
1349.ap: They adapted a state-of-the-art sparse retrieval approach (one that learns which sparse, word-like tokens are important for matching) to music. The key innovation is domain-specific, granular subword tokenization—breaking text into short pieces (max 3 characters). This constraint forces the model to learn actual surface-form robustness (understanding that 'Beathless' and 'Breathless' are variants) rather than memorizing token patterns. Pre-computing embeddings and expansions offline means online processing is just tokenization and fast weighting, adding almost no latency.
1349.wh: Short token constraints (max 3 chars) force the learning objective to generalize: the model can't memorize 'Beathless' as a special case; it must learn the phonetic and character patterns that make it similar to real songs. Pre-computing offline separates the expensive learning phase from online query serving, so latency stays minimal. This is specific to music because music search has unique properties: transpositions, phonetic variations, and abbreviations.
1349.po: On a 6M-document music corpus, the system achieves 91.4% recall@10 versus 57.7% for tri-gram matching, handling misspellings, phonetic variations, and surface-form noise while maintaining millisecond-level latency.
